( Preface to his Kakbarak Ramayana ) M y Soul today retraces the steps in the Kaleidoscope, three score

yei^irs lon^, that it has come through. PYom a tiny village, Nyamalpur. twenty kilometers on fool from the nearest railway station Kishorganja,(now in Bangladesh), it is a long way to be familiar with half-a-dozen University campuses in India. From the village where the educated denizens always remained absent working in distant places and sending only casual cursory letters and regular money orders to their families, where the illiterate and semi-literate old men and women regularly sat around a sickly young boy eveiy af- ternoon to hear him recite the 16th century Rangla Ramayana of Krittibash Ojha (The audience was always the same with one memo- rable exception. Maharaj Trailakya Chakravarti, the revolutionary fire-brand, while in his election campaign, once came to the court- yard, sat quiety behind for half an hour till the chapter was com- plete and patted on the child’s back. That was the greatest admira- tion that he had received till that time.) to the latest renderer of the Ramayana in an upcoming language, is a long way indeed ! The jour- ney has been tortuous, heartbreaking, through desolate heaths, un- der apathy and bemused pity and occasional sympathy. It has been a ‘pilgrim’s progress' though the pilgrim was not always very sure about where he was tnadging to. It is the anecdote of a genuine mediocre who succeeded only then when there were no competitors - from the reciter of the Ramayana in Bangla to the singer of the Ramayana in Kakbarak. in that remote village where 1 was born I was distinguished for cer- tain qualities. Unlike the average children of the village 1 was physi-

|i) cally weak, I was less intelligent than liiosl ot them, 1 had an un- common ability to memorize things effortlessly and 1 had consider- able felicity in rhyming. As 1 was physically weak I was not good enough in games and sports. I could not be ‘unprofitably gay’ in ‘ninning like a doe’. I had a sed- entary habit and my spirit ran for companions in the past. As I was useless in the playground 1 grew a bibliophile. 'Fherc was a large wooden chest in our house that always remained siiut and under an awe-inspiring large lock. I did not know what it contained. But when he noticed my voracity for reading, the casual guest in our house, my father, asked me not to read the books in that magic casket. It was the command of the ‘creator’ not to taste the fruit of the tree of knowledge. He left for his gaol and 1 signed my covenant with Mephistophiles. 1 opened the chest I ran through the writings of Bankimchandra, Saratchandra. Rajkrishna, Srishchandra, Ramesh Chandra Datta, Dinabandhu Mitra, Pyari Chand Mitra and Micha('l Madhusudan Datta. 1 read Saurindramohan’s verse translation of Shakespeare’s works. All this before I Completed my Class VI. 1 had unending hunger for reading but at that age 1 was no connoisseur. I read Haridasher Gupta Katha, Gaurdas Babajir Bhikkhar Jhuli and Sri Chaitanya Chari tamnta with equal zeal. Not that I understood all. Most of these went under my feet or over my head. The mouse gnaws everything into bits and pieces, eats tittle. I read all and the debris of my reading formed the foundation on which grew up the

humble temple of my mediocrity. I was less intelligent tfian the children of my age. This kinship with stupidity ran in the family. My grandfather Kamalakanta was not worldly wise. His altruism led him to poverty which was so acute that my father Rameshchandra could not go for higher education after he passed his Entrance Examination In his anguish he left home, went to Rangoon and got a job there. He earned well. But the inherited bug of doing good to others never allowed him to lay some- thing by. Moreover he managed to establish his relationship with Subhaschandra’s Azad Hind Fauz. He was suspected, nabbed and put into jail. P'or four years he was only a number, a security pris- oner under the care of the C.I.D., D.l.B. etc etc. He was never sent to any court. He came home now and then on parole. He was niy grandfather’s son and with his simplism he believed that the British Government would help his family live well. So he wrote to them to help his family or release him or try him in a court. The Ixird said, ‘Love thy neighbour’. Our neighbours knew it. So when the all-im- portant Sub-Divisional Officer came with his courtiers to investi- gate, our neighbours showed them the large sprawling home we f<i) had, the rows of betel nut trees that yielded cash crops, the plots of land that gave us enough food grains and told them that we were in no way worse off than the average families in the village. The S.D O. departed. But he came to see. So the Government munificence also came, as a fistful of alms, ten rupees a month. Our neighbours were

not amused. ITiat I was a simpleton, 1 gave unquestionable proof many a time. Ihe first one, as 1 recall, was on the first day of my life in school. The teacher asked our names. Four girls told their names and the fifth pupil, 1 said, ‘Srimati Prabhas Chandra Dhar and... This happened over and over again. When 1 began my Kakbarak Ramayana in 1980 people advised me unasked. It was foolish, they said. Why should 1 waste my God-gifted ability (I’m sure that they did not believe it.) in Kakbarak? Who will read it? IVho will buy it? [ could do something in Bangla or English. 1 could give tuition and earn money. As is evi- dent, I was not intelligent enough to listen to them. As a kid 1 was a marvel to the village elders and an exhibit to any stranger for my rote learning rapacity. I memorized all the test books including the book of arithmetic. So when a stranger came I was summoned belore him and was commanded to recite a piece of my text book. I did. But I did not know where to stop. So after gurgling out the ‘Parable of the Good Samaritan* 1 continued: ‘Exercise: One. Wliat is a parable? Two. Wlio was a Samaritan? till I finished ever>*- lliing. 1 did not have the gumption to understand that the listeners (ook me to be a meritorious idiot! 1 do not think that even when 1 am sixty, I have grown any better. I am easily duped. But experience taught me not to mind. Ihe felicity with rhyming is a gift of the soil. Who has not heard of Dinesh Chandra Sen’s collection ‘Maimansingha Gitika’ or the songs from Mymensingh? Wordsw’qrth heard the song of one ‘Solitary

Reaper’, a highland lass in Scotland. But in the district of Mymensingh innumerable songs are born, sung and forgotten eve- ryday. The girls husking the paddy, the women milking the cow or Iransptiuiting the paddy in kneedeep mud and water or dressing the bride for wedding, the men rowing their boats or enjoying their hookah, the Mussalman fakir, the Hindu haul, everyone sings. They quite often sing songs extempore and forget. There are duels of bards in doggerels. So it was not veiy remarkable that I had the ability to versify anything anytime. Tliis ability, however stood me in good stead when I rendered m> Ramayana into Kakbarak or my Raj mala into English. When I was in Class VI my father came home. He was very ill. His condition rapidly deteriorated during the following months. On the day 1 came home from school with the news of my promotion to Class VII, it was 31“^ December, my father was alive only to tcike from me the last teaspoonful of orange Juice. It seemed that he was trying to say something to me. But only a drop of tear rolled down from his right eye and he was no more. My world was totally shat- tered. My studies stopped There was only a Middle English School in the village and I had passed out of that. It was a bad time. My mother began to nurture us three brothers much as the bird-mother nurtures her nestlings. A year passed by. I read and reread the Ramayana and gave epiegesis and epiexegesis of it to my very de- voted and equally uncomprehending greyhaired and credulous au- dience. 1 fidgeted within. But that was my personal matter. The vil-

lage life was calm. The whole subcontinent was. however, in com- motion, the Hindus and Mussalmans were fleeing their lands Paki- stan and India in a scale unprecedented in recorded human history. India won her freedom without much bloodshed. Pakistan was born - cut out of mother India. And after the childbirth there ought to be bleeding even if the child is unwanted. Aurangzib s son was too young to understand why his grandfather was in prison. I was too young in 1950 to understand how Hamid chacha could be our enemy. A valu- able year passed by. slipped off the pufse of my life. It was a rainy day. We were playing football in a small muddy grass- land with a full-grown shaddock as a ball and handfuls of yellow leaves as goalposts. There was a pond at one side and a big hut on the other. In that hut our tailor uncle sat at his sewing machine stitching his shirts and lungis undisturbed by our gleeful shouts now and then. We sometimes felt that the mud was too thick on our bodies to carry on. So we Jumped into the pond and clambered out alter a clumsy wash to resume the kicking game. At that time a man came there. He was wearing a smairt shirt which was not very com- mon in those days. People moved about with a gamcha (a piece of cloth that wiped the body) on their shoulders, or at best a vest on. He went in. sat on a bench and began a conversation with tailor uncle. But I noticed that he had a printed sheet of paper in his hand. My lust for reading anything was immediately roused. So with my mud-bespattered body I went in and standing near tried to espy what the paper was about. The man became irked at my effrontery.

The tailor uncle tried to pacify him telling him about me and my extraordinary love for reading. Yet he growled at me saying that it was the mathematics question paper of that year s Matriculation Examination, no sop for a class sixer. But in the meantime I read out one of the sums and told him the result of it. He was impressed. (iv) He dismissed me from that place and talked with tailor uncle about me. Then he took Initiative and sent me to Itna, a village about twenty kilometers away from our Nyamatpun to the house of the Guptas (One of the Gupta brothers was the famous Bhupesh Gupta who was a member of the Indian Parliament). Dr. Jnanesh Gupta, elder brother of Bhupesh Gupta, accepted me alTectionately and assured me of my boarding and lodging. I stayed in that house for four years. Dr. Jnanesh Gupta became a second father to me. his wife my second mother, his son Sekhar, my best friend. The rela- tionship continues to this day, the senior Guptas are no more though. I passed the Matriculation Examination in 1955. I migrated to India in November 1955. On the day previous to my departure from Nyamatpur for Calcutta 1 went to visit the man who had sent me to Itna four years ago. He was a Mussalman and a god to me. He was an Amirul Islam. When I went to see him he was lying in his bed. He was in fever. He blessed me and assured me saying that Allah would fulfill my desire for reading. 1 would never lack reading materials. Then he said something which remains engraved in my heart in bold black characters. I shall never forget what he

said on that day to me. He said: “How happy 1 could be, if I could sit today on this bed with you and eat our supper together. Don't get frightened. 1 can he^u* your tiny Hindu heart palpitating at the idea of losing your religion. I shall not ask you to do anything of that kind. But in the years to come when you will grow and understand that your religion is not so volatile to vanish at the touch of a morsel of a Mussulman’s food, this unfulfilled desire of mine will haunt you. You shall repent for this that you did not cat with me." Yes, this does haunt me. 1 have travelled through this vast country from Sonemarg to Kanyakumari from Dwarka to Dibrugarh many a time I have eaten at many strange places with diverse friends and stran- gers. But I was a fool in 1955, I dared not to sit and eat with my god because I thought that 1 could love him. respect him but eat with him 1 could not as he was a Mussalman. And he was so great that he excused me even before 1 had time to offend him. I got a job at Agartala in the Directorate of l^nd Records in January 1958. 1 was an Amin Moharar with a salary of Rs. 87.00 when even a lower Division Clerk or a Primary' School Teacher got Rs. 102.50 per month, 'fhen I passed University examinations one after the other till I became an M.A of Calcutta University in 1968. The crawl- ing in the educational line was not very easy. I was a voracious reader indeed. But 1 needed newer pastures. I read Karl Marx, the Mcihabharata and Madame Simone de Beauvoir with equal gusto. Upanishads and Omar Kliaiyam attracted me equally. But reading (V)

the textbooks over and over again for passing the examinations was boring and did not attract me. I was disgusted. In this matter also 1 got God-sent mentors. First, it was a man. an elderly colleague - Amal Majumdar. He loved me and so he would not permit me to waste my time. And he appointed himself my elder brother and forced me to his house to live there so that he could be my guardian to oversee my studies. He is still there at Agartala, my dearest elder brother. Later it was a young woman, a sister of a colleague - Bela. She spurred me constantly on. Then she forced herself to my house to live there so that she could be my guardian to oversee my studies. She is still around, with her goad ever ready to keep the renegade pachyderm in me on the right track. Were she not there my vagrant bonhomie would not allow me to remain in any work for any length of time. Whatever I am today, is largely due to her. In the mean time, as 1 indicated already, 1 married, became a Rev- enue Officer and a father of a daughter - Rupa. In 1969, on the recommendation of the Union Public Service Commision, I got a Lectureship and began to teach English at Maharaja Bir Bikram College, Agartala. A dream came true. Ihe Lord was very kind. I was not required to say: Thy kingdom come.’ He came, at His own will. I got access to the best library in Tripura - my college librar>^ Allah granted me His blessings unasked as Amirul Islam prophesied in 1955. In 1970 my son. Prasun, was born. In 1975 I went to Hyderabad to study Linguistics in the Central Institute of English & Phreign Languages (CIEFL) there. My sojourn

in Hyderabad coincided \Vith the now-infamous Emergency Period. I stayed in that city from July 1975 to March 1977. Working under Dr. Ramakrishna Bansal I acquired the Degree of Master of D^tters (M. Litt.). My other teachers there were such illustrious academi- cians as Dr. S.K. Verma. Dr. M.V. Nadkarni, Dr. T. Balasubrammaniam. Dr. V. Y. Kantak, Dr. B. V. L. N. Rao. Dr. N. Krishnaswarny, Mr. R.K. Tongue and others. Only fortunate people get an opportunity to study under such teachers. The CIF^FL changed rny life’s directions. As I was ushered into the realm of Linguistics and Phonetics my teachers were all full of admi- ration for the Amcrican-European linguists who worked among the Amerindians and recorded their languages meticulously. We knew from our teachers that those linguists were fortunate to find such virgin languages uncontaminated by any previous perfunctoiy dil- ettante. My senses were surcharged and 1 grew ambitious. I knew that I had the opportunity which providence had kept safely guarded for me. Even while I was engaged in my research work in the CIEFL (Vi) my thoughts ran to Tripura to work with Kakbarak - the Language of the majority of the tribal population in the State. After coming back from Hyderabad 1 began to learn Kakbarak. Initially it was in Tripura Rabindra Parishad with Manoranjan Majumdar. 'fhe little book ‘Kakbarak Swrwng’ of Dasarath Deb was of considerable help. But I had countless teachers, 'fhe man who came to College Tilla twice a week to sell charcoal, the workers at Warengbari near

Bishramganj and Rupachera near Tuisindnii. where my brother, Krittibas. worked as a Forest Department Ranger, Budhu DebBarma of wSettlement Office and above all the Kakbarak speaking students in the college year after year were all my teachers. 1 had occasional discussions with and help from the poet -journalist Mahendra DebBarma, the dedicated lover of Kakbarak Alindra Lai Tripura and Narendra Chandra DebBarma. a high official in Akash Vani. Brqjendra Deb Barma, now Security Officer at ;\gart ala Airport was of particular help when he w^as my student . Sri Naresh DebBarma of lYipura legislative Assembly Secretariat helped me ungnidgingly whenever 1 approached him. With my newly acquired knowledge of Linguistics and the tape re- t'order for which tht! money was given by the University Grants Conn mission I began to formalize the grammar ol Kakbarak in modern linguistic lines. The result was a small book ‘Kakbarak Swrwngma’ [niblished by the Directorate of Research in 1983 lliis is the first grammar ol Kakbarak on the basis of modern linguistics. There was a grammar of the language - Kakbarak Ma - written by Radharnohan Thakur published in 1900. But that was, as all grammars of the Aryan languages of India at that lime were, in Sanskritic tradition. Radharnohan Thakur, who w^as a high official in the Maharaja's Government, w^as a versatile genius. It is astonishing that he felt the need of a grammar of Kakbarak and himself did the work. I feel liuinhly proud that I came just after this illustrious Tliakur - eighty years after him - to have dealt with tlic grammar of Kakbarid<. In

1982 I introduced Kakbarak to the wnirld of academicians. In Janu- ary' that year the Intt'rnational Conference of Linguists on South Asian Uinguagcs and Linguistics was held in Mysore in the Central Institute of Indian Uinguages. I presented my paper ‘Adjectives and Numerals in Kakbarak’ there. Since then I presented over a dozen papers on different features of Kcikbarak at diffei ent University semi- nars and conferences held at dilferent places from Guwahati to Annamalai. Many people helped me in many ways. I should mention the name of my student Debapriya DebBarma, at that time Linguis- tic Officer, who got my 1982 paper cyclostyled. From him 1 got the copy of the New Testament of the Bible in Kakbarak - Sinai Kwtal. (vii) This book helped me a great deal In my efforts. Ramaprasad Datta (Paltuda) also helped me in his own way. From 1977 to 1980 I suffered from an intense agony. 1 was dying to do something worthwhile for Kakbarak and I did not have any clear idea of what 1 should do. The nineteenth centuiy Amerlcan-Euro- pean Linguists could not give me any lead. My object was totally different from theirs. They meticulously recorded the many Amerin- dian languages which they allowed to die their natural death of as- phyxia under the tremendous pressure of English. Most of those languages remain now in their mummified state in those meticu- lous records only. My intention was diametrically opposite. 1 intended to invigorate Kakbarak, to give such directions to it that would make the learning/ teaching of the language effortless, to help Kakbarak

by giving it something great which would become an object of pride for the speakers of the language. But my thoughts floated like iri- descent bubbles on a placid lake during rains: they made endless shapes and patterns, disappeared and reappeared. My desire re- mained unfulfilled. While 1 was writhing in my labour pain 1 read an article on Viswanatha Satyanarayana, the Telugu poet and his Ramayana Kalpavrlksha. It worked like a miracle cure. I remem- bered my adolescent companion - the Bangla Ramayema of the le'** century poet-saint Krlttibas Ojha. The Ramayana of Valmiki moulds the Indian psyche even today - many thousand years after it was composed. When the Bible was translated into the modern European languages - in the 15th through 17th centuries - the Ramayana was also translated into the Sanskritic languages (Kamban Ramayana in Tamil is far older, it belongs to the 9th/ 10th century.) of India. The translators of the Ramayana - Kamban, Madhav Kundali, Krittibas OJha, Goswami Tulsidas and others have all become sages to us Indians. The Ramayana in trans- lation forms the foundation of all the modern languages of North India. Tire Ramayana in Kakbarak will help the development of the language at a greater pace. It will give the Kakbarak speaker a first- hand knowledge of his heritage - a heritage which is older and greater than any other in this world. It will enrich the vocabulary of the Icinguage. It will be a possession of pride for the speakers of the language. It will help national Integration in a better way. I began the work of rendering the Ramayana into Kakbarak. I worked

relentlessly for ten years on it. Krittibas’s Ramayana is a stupen- dous work in Bangla. Thirty-six thousand lines in lilting couplets and triplets. The emotions of affection, love and hate, of valour, cru- elty, meanness and greatness have been Incomparably given expres- (vlll) Sion to in it. Therefore it is a classic in Bangla and a possession of pride for the Bengalees. In the meantime I registered my name as a research scholar for the Degree of Ph. D. of Calcutta University and quietly constructed my dissertation for it. There is a proverb in Hindi which means that when God wants to give no barrier can bar. His gift comes through the roof. In my life it happened repeatedly. There is no limit to His mercy that rained upon me. In Ihe academic circle a Ph. D. degree is a prestigious mark of distinction. The greatest hurdle on the way to reach this glory gar- land is to find a guide - unless one gets a regular Fellowship in a University. In that case the University provides the Fellow with a scholarship, an adequate library facility and a Guide. But for others getting a Guide is a veritable problem. My case was different. Dr. Kartik Lahiri was an elderly colleague in my college. A literateur of considerable fame Dr. Lahiri was a venerated personage in the elite society of Agartala. He began to admonish me for not using my studies in a disciplined way. This continued for a couple of years. God sent him to help me. At last I told him that I would work if he agreed to be my Guide. He Eigreed. The result was the conferment of the degree of Ph. D. upon me by Calcutta University in 1993.

Isvarah sarvabhutdnang hriddese cujuna tistati Bhramayan sarvabhutdni yantrdruddjxi mdyayd. Arjuna, God abides in the heart of all creatures, causing them to revolve according to their Karma by His illusive power, seated as those beings are in the vehicle of the body. When I saw that my work was complete I ca '.led in some of my friends to my house to let them know what I had done during the preceding ten years. There were Dr. Saiju Tewari, Ms. Karabl DebBarma. Dr. Nilraani DebBarma. Anil DebBarma. Bijan Krishna Chaudhuii among others. They all appreciated my work. They added that it was a good work but it could be better still if 1 could put it in the Krittibashl framework - a work of fourteen syllables In every line of the cou- plets. The suggestion was good. But ,was it workable? 1 sat down to tiy. Six years I spent again in reshaping the lines, rewriting all the thirty- six thousand lines again. I don’t know how many kilos of paper 1 tore, cramped and threw away in disgust. But it was complete in 1995. Bijan Krishna Chaudhuri was no more to see it. Dr. Saiju Tlwari retired and went home - Gazipur near Varanasi. Many people helped me in many ways. Those who spoke a few encouraging words now and then were like the bystanders for a marathon runner. TTiey offer a glass of water or a chewing gum or just say a cheering word. But their help is priceless. How many will I name? Ms. Rajlaxmi Chaudhurl, Prlyabrata Bhattachaijee. the late Prof. Suhas Chatteijee of Calcutta University were always kind to ask how far 1 advanced in

my journey. Many people helped when they sat with me to read or listen to my Ramayana and to give their suggestions. Sister Bina Reang, Late Mahendra DebBarma. my students Chandra Krishna Malsum of Kalyan Ashram and Madhuiya Kalai of Baisyamanipara. Noaram Tripura of Fulchari, Ranjan De of Kalyan Ashram, the large audience at Chhaomanu and Dhumachhara who listened when 1 read my Ramayana and applauded, and cheered lustily, my col- league Prof Mebar Jamatia. Rajendra DebBarma and Bijay DebBarma of Agartala Employment Exchange come to this group. In this soli- tary journey I got encouragement and blessings from Swami Vlshnupuriji Maharaj and Swami Kripalananda Glri maharaj also. Buddha DebBarma. Kashiram Reang and Negendra Jamatia - all former ministers of Tripura - were kind to see some portions of my Ramaytma and say a few kind words to encourage me. I shall re- main always grateful to all of them. My friend Dr. Prasanta Kumar Bhattachaijee took me to these political luminaries. The encourag- ing words of Dr Satyen Goswami. Rabindranath Tagore Professor. Gauhatl University always inspired me. The members of the Adhyatma Vljnan Parishad with Dr Sumangal Sen have always been sympathetic. As soon eis my Ramayana was ready to go to the Press, Mr. D. K. lyagi. the then Commissioner in charge of the Departments of Edu- cation and Tnbal Resejireh heard about it and he took it to publish. When the manuscript was ready to go to the printer something mys- terious happened somewhere and the ongoing machine stopped

abruptly. Nobody let me know why. Mr. lyagl was transferred and he left for his new place of posting - New Delhi. 1 always got the blessings of Saraswatl. the goddess of learning and wisdom, in profusion. But Laxmidevi. the goddess ol wealth and power, has always been thrifty. True, she never put me to starva- tion. But she has not been very generous. So when the enthusiasm in the government publishing organ suddenly turned cool 1 was face to face with reality, the problem of money. The printing of the Ramayana would require much more monCy than what I saved through my life. What could I do? Would all my efforts for sixteen long years go in vain? Many people came forward with their mite. My wife Bela wanted to sell everything she had to add to our sav- ings. My son wanted to get loan from his work-place. My friend (X) Dhuijatl Prasad Gupta came to donate Rs. 5000.00 to the ‘Ramayana Printing Fund’! Ms. Rajlaxml Chaudhuri offered her bangles. Putuldi, a retired teacher living on her meagre pension, came quietly with Rs. 301.00 to help me. My eyes get wet when I think of jQl the kind- ness of the people that rained upon me to cool my worries. I re- quested everyone to wait till I could gather courage enough to launch this publishing project which might turn out heavier than 1 could bear. Balaram Santra of Kalyan Ashram, Agartala was one of the few quiet admirers who would like to see the Ramayana in print. At his request Kripa Prasad Slnghji of All India Vanbasi Kalyan Ashram. Jashpur made endeavours for a whole year to find out some benevo-

lent sponsor to donate some mon^ to help publish the Ramayana for the benefit of the tribal people of Tripura. But God willed not that way. In this grave crisis also He gave me courage not to lose heart and to say, "Thy will be done.’ Meanwhile I got a commission to translate the third volume of Sri Rajmala into English. Sri Rajmala is the history of Tripura and her Kings written in Bangla rhyming couplets by Gangadhar Siddhanta Bagish in the 1 7“* century. I rendered it into English verse line by line. It was published in 1995. 1 wsis asked by an esoteric group to translate into Kakbarak the gem of a booklet, 'Manav Dharma’, an edited version of an enlightening lecture delivered by a young Re- search Scholar in Chicago. U.S.A. in 1933. The speaker has grown to be the scholar-extraordinary and saint, Mahanambrata Brahmachari. I did. It will be published soon. When the state of affairs was in such toteil confusion my friends asked me to approach the Ministers. But I could not do so. My rea- sons may sound foolish to many. But 1 have confessed already that I had been less intelligent than everyone: it ran in the family. 1 con- fess again that I have been a Lotus Eater all through my life. 1 lived in a sort of dreamland, far from reality. I did not pay heed to ray counselors who advised me not to waste my time and energy in this unreal, unworkable, good for-nothing venture. So 1 am now at this juncture. I have wasted my genius and my youth, 1 denied my family the happiness that money can buy and now 1 am nowhere. If the Ramayana cannot be published for want of money the termites would

feed upon the manuscript. No one will know about it. Yet it is a unique work. The Ramayana has been translated into many of the large world languages. But of the hundreds of tribal languages of the world not even one has a complete Ramayana in it. If published, my Kakbarak Ramayana in verse could make history. Another five hundred years would pass for another Lotus Eater to be born, to waste his youth and genius, to work with the Ramayana with his (xl) indefatigable optimism, to try to help Kakbarak to develop, and when his work will be complete, to And the government publishing organ suddenly turn cool and his manuscript become good for nothing. I should have tried to meet the Ministers; I could not. Agartala is a small place. Itiere are advantages and disadvantages of living in a small place. Advantages are that there almost everyone is known to others. The present Chief Minister was my student in his college days. The present Education Minister was a very good friend. 1 can go to meet them without much effort and request them to help me out of my crisis. It is possible that they would. But there is a disad- vantage also. There could be some difficulty for which they might not help me. I would irrationally think that they did not help me although they could. So the Lotus Eater in me did not permit me to approach the Ministers for help. Wordsworth would not go to visit Yarrow lest the picture he painted in his heart of Yarrow be broken at the touch of reality. 1 did not go fo approach the highest authori- ties in the government for the same reeison. I would rather keep the

belief in my heart that they would help me if 1 did ask for it. By July 1998 my stars seemed to change their position in the con- stellation. My crisis began to recede. As I am due to retire in Febru- ary 2000, I got my gratuity, provident fund, savings etc. calculated to see whether the whole amount would be adequate for the printing of the Ramayana. Then I and my wife went to Subal Kumar De, the Editor of the Syandan Patrlka. He has always been a younger brother to me. We told him everything and wanted to know the position; the money that 1 expected t© get vis-a-vis the expenditure to be incurred in the printing. My wife added that he was not merely a brother-in- law, he was like a son to her. The calculations should be very real. We have no other means to meet any unforeseen shortfall. He smiled and said something the like of which nobody else could say. He said, “Don’t worry. It will be printed. It is a national duty. Everyone should help. Give it to me It will be done.” The burden of the Himalayas, as it were, was taken off from my chest. Tlie work began. About a week after that Agni Kumar Acharjee, the retired Deputy Secretary of Tripura Public Service Commlslon and Gaurdas Saha of Parul Prakashani came to me on a certain errand. The Ramayana cropped up during conversation. 1 told them everything including our meeting Subal Kumar De. They were interested. They told me that they would try to help me. Gaurdas said that it would be diffi- cult to publish a 600 page book from Agartala. Agni Babu and Gaurdas apprised Mr. Jauhourie, the Station Director, Door Darshan Kendra. Agartala of my Ramayana. He was very kind to take Interest

in the matter. He got an interview with me about my Ramayana. It (xli) was later telecast from Agartala Kendra. 1 told Subal about Gaurdas’ apprehension. He appreciated and stopped the work at Agartala. The scene shifted to Calcutta. All this happened in quick succession - as if in a dream. Gaurdas took the charge of the whole thing auid got it done. He led me through the darkness to light. When 1 was very young cmd my father was only a casual visitor to our house 1 was under the charge of my grandmother. She was my mentor and she moulded my character as she wanted. 1 do not re- member her figure very well today. But I have many of her sayings imprinted in my soul. 1 follow her instructions instinctively. She asked me to bow my head to all places of worship irrespective of the religion. She advised me never to ask for anything from God be- cause He is so big a giver that whaterver I ask for would appear ridiculously trivial. She instructed me to pray to God to keep every- one happy so that no one would need to seek my help which 1 may not be able to render. She asked me to be always content because God is always just and He gives everyone according to his needs and as he deserves. I am content. 1 have come through many vicissitudes. Yet 1 am con- tent. What is life if there is no battle to fight? 1 fought, lost and won. I have a darling of a daughter, a sagacious son, both happily mar- ried. The son-in-law, Basab and the daughter-in-law, Mudita are delectable persons 1 have a jewel of a grandson, my daughter’s son,

Sanket. 1 have my two devoted brothers - Dipankar and Krittlbas - and their families. 1 have am uncompromising, undemanding wife to look after me through weal and woe. 1 have numberless friends and well wishers. 1 have no enemies. Enemies are bom of wealth and power and I have none. 1 bear no ill will to anybody. 1 adways try to “take praise and reproach alike, remain in contemplation and be contented in anything and everything." tidyanindilsIxitiTrnaimi santusto yena kenachit My Ramayana is finally printed. Thanks to the composers amd the printers. They did a marvelous job in an unknown language. 1 hope all that 1 meamt it for will come tme. Kaikbarak speakers will read ir centuries after my generation will have sunk into oblivion. 1 shaU retire In Februairy 2000. Vanaprastha at laist. 1 do not know how mamy days are left in my life’s acount. Given the time 1 have the desire to constmct a Kakbauak - Bamgla amd a Bangla - Kadcbaraik Dlctlonauy. 1 also intend to work for a Comprehensive Graunmau- of the Chaikma Lamguaige. 1 only wish. I shadl have time for aill that. Should summons come before 1 complete the works 1 shadl leave them for someone else to do. (xill) I say to everyone : Thank you I am grateful to you for all the kind words and deeds you said and did unto me. 1 say to the maker of eveiyone : Thy will be done - Kanshye vachanang taba. JAIRAM Mahashivaratri

( Preface to his Kakbarak Ramayana ) M y Soul today retraces the steps in the Kaleidoscope, three score

yei^irs lon^, that it has come through. PYom a tiny village, Nyamalpur. twenty kilometers on fool from the nearest railway station Kishorganja,(now in Bangladesh), it is a long way to be familiar with half-a-dozen University campuses in India. From the village where the educated denizens always remained absent working in distant places and sending only casual cursory letters and regular money orders to their families, where the illiterate and semi-literate old men and women regularly sat around a sickly young boy eveiy af- ternoon to hear him recite the 16th century Rangla Ramayana of Krittibash Ojha (The audience was always the same with one memo- rable exception. Maharaj Trailakya Chakravarti, the revolutionary fire-brand, while in his election campaign, once came to the court- yard, sat quiety behind for half an hour till the chapter was com- plete and patted on the child’s back. That was the greatest admira- tion that he had received till that time.) to the latest renderer of the Ramayana in an upcoming language, is a long way indeed ! The jour- ney has been tortuous, heartbreaking, through desolate heaths, un- der apathy and bemused pity and occasional sympathy. It has been a ‘pilgrim’s progress' though the pilgrim was not always very sure about where he was tnadging to. It is the anecdote of a genuine mediocre who succeeded only then when there were no competitors - from the reciter of the Ramayana in Bangla to the singer of the Ramayana in Kakbarak. in that remote village where 1 was born I was distinguished for cer- tain qualities. Unlike the average children of the village 1 was physi-

|i) cally weak, I was less intelligent than liiosl ot them, 1 had an un- common ability to memorize things effortlessly and 1 had consider- able felicity in rhyming. As 1 was physically weak I was not good enough in games and sports. I could not be ‘unprofitably gay’ in ‘ninning like a doe’. I had a sed- entary habit and my spirit ran for companions in the past. As I was useless in the playground 1 grew a bibliophile. 'Fherc was a large wooden chest in our house that always remained siiut and under an awe-inspiring large lock. I did not know what it contained. But when he noticed my voracity for reading, the casual guest in our house, my father, asked me not to read the books in that magic casket. It was the command of the ‘creator’ not to taste the fruit of the tree of knowledge. He left for his gaol and 1 signed my covenant with Mephistophiles. 1 opened the chest I ran through the writings of Bankimchandra, Saratchandra. Rajkrishna, Srishchandra, Ramesh Chandra Datta, Dinabandhu Mitra, Pyari Chand Mitra and Micha('l Madhusudan Datta. 1 read Saurindramohan’s verse translation of Shakespeare’s works. All this before I Completed my Class VI. 1 had unending hunger for reading but at that age 1 was no connoisseur. I read Haridasher Gupta Katha, Gaurdas Babajir Bhikkhar Jhuli and Sri Chaitanya Chari tamnta with equal zeal. Not that I understood all. Most of these went under my feet or over my head. The mouse gnaws everything into bits and pieces, eats tittle. I read all and the debris of my reading formed the foundation on which grew up the

humble temple of my mediocrity. I was less intelligent tfian the children of my age. This kinship with stupidity ran in the family. My grandfather Kamalakanta was not worldly wise. His altruism led him to poverty which was so acute that my father Rameshchandra could not go for higher education after he passed his Entrance Examination In his anguish he left home, went to Rangoon and got a job there. He earned well. But the inherited bug of doing good to others never allowed him to lay some- thing by. Moreover he managed to establish his relationship with Subhaschandra’s Azad Hind Fauz. He was suspected, nabbed and put into jail. P'or four years he was only a number, a security pris- oner under the care of the C.I.D., D.l.B. etc etc. He was never sent to any court. He came home now and then on parole. He was niy grandfather’s son and with his simplism he believed that the British Government would help his family live well. So he wrote to them to help his family or release him or try him in a court. The Ixird said, ‘Love thy neighbour’. Our neighbours knew it. So when the all-im- portant Sub-Divisional Officer came with his courtiers to investi- gate, our neighbours showed them the large sprawling home we f<i) had, the rows of betel nut trees that yielded cash crops, the plots of land that gave us enough food grains and told them that we were in no way worse off than the average families in the village. The S.D O. departed. But he came to see. So the Government munificence also came, as a fistful of alms, ten rupees a month. Our neighbours were

not amused. ITiat I was a simpleton, 1 gave unquestionable proof many a time. Ihe first one, as 1 recall, was on the first day of my life in school. The teacher asked our names. Four girls told their names and the fifth pupil, 1 said, ‘Srimati Prabhas Chandra Dhar and... This happened over and over again. When 1 began my Kakbarak Ramayana in 1980 people advised me unasked. It was foolish, they said. Why should 1 waste my God-gifted ability (I’m sure that they did not believe it.) in Kakbarak? Who will read it? IVho will buy it? [ could do something in Bangla or English. 1 could give tuition and earn money. As is evi- dent, I was not intelligent enough to listen to them. As a kid 1 was a marvel to the village elders and an exhibit to any stranger for my rote learning rapacity. I memorized all the test books including the book of arithmetic. So when a stranger came I was summoned belore him and was commanded to recite a piece of my text book. I did. But I did not know where to stop. So after gurgling out the ‘Parable of the Good Samaritan* 1 continued: ‘Exercise: One. Wliat is a parable? Two. Wlio was a Samaritan? till I finished ever>*- lliing. 1 did not have the gumption to understand that the listeners (ook me to be a meritorious idiot! 1 do not think that even when 1 am sixty, I have grown any better. I am easily duped. But experience taught me not to mind. Ihe felicity with rhyming is a gift of the soil. Who has not heard of Dinesh Chandra Sen’s collection ‘Maimansingha Gitika’ or the songs from Mymensingh? Wordsw’qrth heard the song of one ‘Solitary

Reaper’, a highland lass in Scotland. But in the district of Mymensingh innumerable songs are born, sung and forgotten eve- ryday. The girls husking the paddy, the women milking the cow or Iransptiuiting the paddy in kneedeep mud and water or dressing the bride for wedding, the men rowing their boats or enjoying their hookah, the Mussalman fakir, the Hindu haul, everyone sings. They quite often sing songs extempore and forget. There are duels of bards in doggerels. So it was not veiy remarkable that I had the ability to versify anything anytime. Tliis ability, however stood me in good stead when I rendered m> Ramayana into Kakbarak or my Raj mala into English. When I was in Class VI my father came home. He was very ill. His condition rapidly deteriorated during the following months. On the day 1 came home from school with the news of my promotion to Class VII, it was 31“^ December, my father was alive only to tcike from me the last teaspoonful of orange Juice. It seemed that he was trying to say something to me. But only a drop of tear rolled down from his right eye and he was no more. My world was totally shat- tered. My studies stopped There was only a Middle English School in the village and I had passed out of that. It was a bad time. My mother began to nurture us three brothers much as the bird-mother nurtures her nestlings. A year passed by. I read and reread the Ramayana and gave epiegesis and epiexegesis of it to my very de- voted and equally uncomprehending greyhaired and credulous au- dience. 1 fidgeted within. But that was my personal matter. The vil-

lage life was calm. The whole subcontinent was. however, in com- motion, the Hindus and Mussalmans were fleeing their lands Paki- stan and India in a scale unprecedented in recorded human history. India won her freedom without much bloodshed. Pakistan was born - cut out of mother India. And after the childbirth there ought to be bleeding even if the child is unwanted. Aurangzib s son was too young to understand why his grandfather was in prison. I was too young in 1950 to understand how Hamid chacha could be our enemy. A valu- able year passed by. slipped off the pufse of my life. It was a rainy day. We were playing football in a small muddy grass- land with a full-grown shaddock as a ball and handfuls of yellow leaves as goalposts. There was a pond at one side and a big hut on the other. In that hut our tailor uncle sat at his sewing machine stitching his shirts and lungis undisturbed by our gleeful shouts now and then. We sometimes felt that the mud was too thick on our bodies to carry on. So we Jumped into the pond and clambered out alter a clumsy wash to resume the kicking game. At that time a man came there. He was wearing a smairt shirt which was not very com- mon in those days. People moved about with a gamcha (a piece of cloth that wiped the body) on their shoulders, or at best a vest on. He went in. sat on a bench and began a conversation with tailor uncle. But I noticed that he had a printed sheet of paper in his hand. My lust for reading anything was immediately roused. So with my mud-bespattered body I went in and standing near tried to espy what the paper was about. The man became irked at my effrontery.

The tailor uncle tried to pacify him telling him about me and my extraordinary love for reading. Yet he growled at me saying that it was the mathematics question paper of that year s Matriculation Examination, no sop for a class sixer. But in the meantime I read out one of the sums and told him the result of it. He was impressed. (iv) He dismissed me from that place and talked with tailor uncle about me. Then he took Initiative and sent me to Itna, a village about twenty kilometers away from our Nyamatpun to the house of the Guptas (One of the Gupta brothers was the famous Bhupesh Gupta who was a member of the Indian Parliament). Dr. Jnanesh Gupta, elder brother of Bhupesh Gupta, accepted me alTectionately and assured me of my boarding and lodging. I stayed in that house for four years. Dr. Jnanesh Gupta became a second father to me. his wife my second mother, his son Sekhar, my best friend. The rela- tionship continues to this day, the senior Guptas are no more though. I passed the Matriculation Examination in 1955. I migrated to India in November 1955. On the day previous to my departure from Nyamatpur for Calcutta 1 went to visit the man who had sent me to Itna four years ago. He was a Mussalman and a god to me. He was an Amirul Islam. When I went to see him he was lying in his bed. He was in fever. He blessed me and assured me saying that Allah would fulfill my desire for reading. 1 would never lack reading materials. Then he said something which remains engraved in my heart in bold black characters. I shall never forget what he

said on that day to me. He said: “How happy 1 could be, if I could sit today on this bed with you and eat our supper together. Don't get frightened. 1 can he^u* your tiny Hindu heart palpitating at the idea of losing your religion. I shall not ask you to do anything of that kind. But in the years to come when you will grow and understand that your religion is not so volatile to vanish at the touch of a morsel of a Mussulman’s food, this unfulfilled desire of mine will haunt you. You shall repent for this that you did not cat with me." Yes, this does haunt me. 1 have travelled through this vast country from Sonemarg to Kanyakumari from Dwarka to Dibrugarh many a time I have eaten at many strange places with diverse friends and stran- gers. But I was a fool in 1955, I dared not to sit and eat with my god because I thought that 1 could love him. respect him but eat with him 1 could not as he was a Mussalman. And he was so great that he excused me even before 1 had time to offend him. I got a job at Agartala in the Directorate of l^nd Records in January 1958. 1 was an Amin Moharar with a salary of Rs. 87.00 when even a lower Division Clerk or a Primary' School Teacher got Rs. 102.50 per month, 'fhen I passed University examinations one after the other till I became an M.A of Calcutta University in 1968. The crawl- ing in the educational line was not very easy. I was a voracious reader indeed. But 1 needed newer pastures. I read Karl Marx, the Mcihabharata and Madame Simone de Beauvoir with equal gusto. Upanishads and Omar Kliaiyam attracted me equally. But reading (V)

the textbooks over and over again for passing the examinations was boring and did not attract me. I was disgusted. In this matter also 1 got God-sent mentors. First, it was a man. an elderly colleague - Amal Majumdar. He loved me and so he would not permit me to waste my time. And he appointed himself my elder brother and forced me to his house to live there so that he could be my guardian to oversee my studies. He is still there at Agartala, my dearest elder brother. Later it was a young woman, a sister of a colleague - Bela. She spurred me constantly on. Then she forced herself to my house to live there so that she could be my guardian to oversee my studies. She is still around, with her goad ever ready to keep the renegade pachyderm in me on the right track. Were she not there my vagrant bonhomie would not allow me to remain in any work for any length of time. Whatever I am today, is largely due to her. In the mean time, as 1 indicated already, 1 married, became a Rev- enue Officer and a father of a daughter - Rupa. In 1969, on the recommendation of the Union Public Service Commision, I got a Lectureship and began to teach English at Maharaja Bir Bikram College, Agartala. A dream came true. Ihe Lord was very kind. I was not required to say: Thy kingdom come.’ He came, at His own will. I got access to the best library in Tripura - my college librar>^ Allah granted me His blessings unasked as Amirul Islam prophesied in 1955. In 1970 my son. Prasun, was born. In 1975 I went to Hyderabad to study Linguistics in the Central Institute of English & Phreign Languages (CIEFL) there. My sojourn

in Hyderabad coincided \Vith the now-infamous Emergency Period. I stayed in that city from July 1975 to March 1977. Working under Dr. Ramakrishna Bansal I acquired the Degree of Master of D^tters (M. Litt.). My other teachers there were such illustrious academi- cians as Dr. S.K. Verma. Dr. M.V. Nadkarni, Dr. T. Balasubrammaniam. Dr. V. Y. Kantak, Dr. B. V. L. N. Rao. Dr. N. Krishnaswarny, Mr. R.K. Tongue and others. Only fortunate people get an opportunity to study under such teachers. The CIF^FL changed rny life’s directions. As I was ushered into the realm of Linguistics and Phonetics my teachers were all full of admi- ration for the Amcrican-European linguists who worked among the Amerindians and recorded their languages meticulously. We knew from our teachers that those linguists were fortunate to find such virgin languages uncontaminated by any previous perfunctoiy dil- ettante. My senses were surcharged and 1 grew ambitious. I knew that I had the opportunity which providence had kept safely guarded for me. Even while I was engaged in my research work in the CIEFL (Vi) my thoughts ran to Tripura to work with Kakbarak - the Language of the majority of the tribal population in the State. After coming back from Hyderabad 1 began to learn Kakbarak. Initially it was in Tripura Rabindra Parishad with Manoranjan Majumdar. 'fhe little book ‘Kakbarak Swrwng’ of Dasarath Deb was of considerable help. But I had countless teachers, 'fhe man who came to College Tilla twice a week to sell charcoal, the workers at Warengbari near

Bishramganj and Rupachera near Tuisindnii. where my brother, Krittibas. worked as a Forest Department Ranger, Budhu DebBarma of wSettlement Office and above all the Kakbarak speaking students in the college year after year were all my teachers. 1 had occasional discussions with and help from the poet -journalist Mahendra DebBarma, the dedicated lover of Kakbarak Alindra Lai Tripura and Narendra Chandra DebBarma. a high official in Akash Vani. Brqjendra Deb Barma, now Security Officer at ;\gart ala Airport was of particular help when he w^as my student . Sri Naresh DebBarma of lYipura legislative Assembly Secretariat helped me ungnidgingly whenever 1 approached him. With my newly acquired knowledge of Linguistics and the tape re- t'order for which tht! money was given by the University Grants Conn mission I began to formalize the grammar ol Kakbarak in modern linguistic lines. The result was a small book ‘Kakbarak Swrwngma’ [niblished by the Directorate of Research in 1983 lliis is the first grammar ol Kakbarak on the basis of modern linguistics. There was a grammar of the language - Kakbarak Ma - written by Radharnohan Thakur published in 1900. But that was, as all grammars of the Aryan languages of India at that lime were, in Sanskritic tradition. Radharnohan Thakur, who w^as a high official in the Maharaja's Government, w^as a versatile genius. It is astonishing that he felt the need of a grammar of Kakbarak and himself did the work. I feel liuinhly proud that I came just after this illustrious Tliakur - eighty years after him - to have dealt with tlic grammar of Kakbarid<. In

1982 I introduced Kakbarak to the wnirld of academicians. In Janu- ary' that year the Intt'rnational Conference of Linguists on South Asian Uinguagcs and Linguistics was held in Mysore in the Central Institute of Indian Uinguages. I presented my paper ‘Adjectives and Numerals in Kakbarak’ there. Since then I presented over a dozen papers on different features of Kcikbarak at diffei ent University semi- nars and conferences held at dilferent places from Guwahati to Annamalai. Many people helped me in many ways. I should mention the name of my student Debapriya DebBarma, at that time Linguis- tic Officer, who got my 1982 paper cyclostyled. From him 1 got the copy of the New Testament of the Bible in Kakbarak - Sinai Kwtal. (vii) This book helped me a great deal In my efforts. Ramaprasad Datta (Paltuda) also helped me in his own way. From 1977 to 1980 I suffered from an intense agony. 1 was dying to do something worthwhile for Kakbarak and I did not have any clear idea of what 1 should do. The nineteenth centuiy Amerlcan-Euro- pean Linguists could not give me any lead. My object was totally different from theirs. They meticulously recorded the many Amerin- dian languages which they allowed to die their natural death of as- phyxia under the tremendous pressure of English. Most of those languages remain now in their mummified state in those meticu- lous records only. My intention was diametrically opposite. 1 intended to invigorate Kakbarak, to give such directions to it that would make the learning/ teaching of the language effortless, to help Kakbarak

by giving it something great which would become an object of pride for the speakers of the language. But my thoughts floated like iri- descent bubbles on a placid lake during rains: they made endless shapes and patterns, disappeared and reappeared. My desire re- mained unfulfilled. While 1 was writhing in my labour pain 1 read an article on Viswanatha Satyanarayana, the Telugu poet and his Ramayana Kalpavrlksha. It worked like a miracle cure. I remem- bered my adolescent companion - the Bangla Ramayema of the le'** century poet-saint Krlttibas Ojha. The Ramayana of Valmiki moulds the Indian psyche even today - many thousand years after it was composed. When the Bible was translated into the modern European languages - in the 15th through 17th centuries - the Ramayana was also translated into the Sanskritic languages (Kamban Ramayana in Tamil is far older, it belongs to the 9th/ 10th century.) of India. The translators of the Ramayana - Kamban, Madhav Kundali, Krittibas OJha, Goswami Tulsidas and others have all become sages to us Indians. The Ramayana in trans- lation forms the foundation of all the modern languages of North India. Tire Ramayana in Kakbarak will help the development of the language at a greater pace. It will give the Kakbarak speaker a first- hand knowledge of his heritage - a heritage which is older and greater than any other in this world. It will enrich the vocabulary of the Icinguage. It will be a possession of pride for the speakers of the language. It will help national Integration in a better way. I began the work of rendering the Ramayana into Kakbarak. I worked

relentlessly for ten years on it. Krittibas’s Ramayana is a stupen- dous work in Bangla. Thirty-six thousand lines in lilting couplets and triplets. The emotions of affection, love and hate, of valour, cru- elty, meanness and greatness have been Incomparably given expres- (vlll) Sion to in it. Therefore it is a classic in Bangla and a possession of pride for the Bengalees. In the meantime I registered my name as a research scholar for the Degree of Ph. D. of Calcutta University and quietly constructed my dissertation for it. There is a proverb in Hindi which means that when God wants to give no barrier can bar. His gift comes through the roof. In my life it happened repeatedly. There is no limit to His mercy that rained upon me. In Ihe academic circle a Ph. D. degree is a prestigious mark of distinction. The greatest hurdle on the way to reach this glory gar- land is to find a guide - unless one gets a regular Fellowship in a University. In that case the University provides the Fellow with a scholarship, an adequate library facility and a Guide. But for others getting a Guide is a veritable problem. My case was different. Dr. Kartik Lahiri was an elderly colleague in my college. A literateur of considerable fame Dr. Lahiri was a venerated personage in the elite society of Agartala. He began to admonish me for not using my studies in a disciplined way. This continued for a couple of years. God sent him to help me. At last I told him that I would work if he agreed to be my Guide. He Eigreed. The result was the conferment of the degree of Ph. D. upon me by Calcutta University in 1993.

Isvarah sarvabhutdnang hriddese cujuna tistati Bhramayan sarvabhutdni yantrdruddjxi mdyayd. Arjuna, God abides in the heart of all creatures, causing them to revolve according to their Karma by His illusive power, seated as those beings are in the vehicle of the body. When I saw that my work was complete I ca '.led in some of my friends to my house to let them know what I had done during the preceding ten years. There were Dr. Saiju Tewari, Ms. Karabl DebBarma. Dr. Nilraani DebBarma. Anil DebBarma. Bijan Krishna Chaudhuii among others. They all appreciated my work. They added that it was a good work but it could be better still if 1 could put it in the Krittibashl framework - a work of fourteen syllables In every line of the cou- plets. The suggestion was good. But ,was it workable? 1 sat down to tiy. Six years I spent again in reshaping the lines, rewriting all the thirty- six thousand lines again. I don’t know how many kilos of paper 1 tore, cramped and threw away in disgust. But it was complete in 1995. Bijan Krishna Chaudhuri was no more to see it. Dr. Saiju Tlwari retired and went home - Gazipur near Varanasi. Many people helped me in many ways. Those who spoke a few encouraging words now and then were like the bystanders for a marathon runner. TTiey offer a glass of water or a chewing gum or just say a cheering word. But their help is priceless. How many will I name? Ms. Rajlaxmi Chaudhurl, Prlyabrata Bhattachaijee. the late Prof. Suhas Chatteijee of Calcutta University were always kind to ask how far 1 advanced in

my journey. Many people helped when they sat with me to read or listen to my Ramayana and to give their suggestions. Sister Bina Reang, Late Mahendra DebBarma. my students Chandra Krishna Malsum of Kalyan Ashram and Madhuiya Kalai of Baisyamanipara. Noaram Tripura of Fulchari, Ranjan De of Kalyan Ashram, the large audience at Chhaomanu and Dhumachhara who listened when 1 read my Ramayana and applauded, and cheered lustily, my col- league Prof Mebar Jamatia. Rajendra DebBarma and Bijay DebBarma of Agartala Employment Exchange come to this group. In this soli- tary journey I got encouragement and blessings from Swami Vlshnupuriji Maharaj and Swami Kripalananda Glri maharaj also. Buddha DebBarma. Kashiram Reang and Negendra Jamatia - all former ministers of Tripura - were kind to see some portions of my Ramaytma and say a few kind words to encourage me. I shall re- main always grateful to all of them. My friend Dr. Prasanta Kumar Bhattachaijee took me to these political luminaries. The encourag- ing words of Dr Satyen Goswami. Rabindranath Tagore Professor. Gauhatl University always inspired me. The members of the Adhyatma Vljnan Parishad with Dr Sumangal Sen have always been sympathetic. As soon eis my Ramayana was ready to go to the Press, Mr. D. K. lyagi. the then Commissioner in charge of the Departments of Edu- cation and Tnbal Resejireh heard about it and he took it to publish. When the manuscript was ready to go to the printer something mys- terious happened somewhere and the ongoing machine stopped

abruptly. Nobody let me know why. Mr. lyagl was transferred and he left for his new place of posting - New Delhi. 1 always got the blessings of Saraswatl. the goddess of learning and wisdom, in profusion. But Laxmidevi. the goddess ol wealth and power, has always been thrifty. True, she never put me to starva- tion. But she has not been very generous. So when the enthusiasm in the government publishing organ suddenly turned cool 1 was face to face with reality, the problem of money. The printing of the Ramayana would require much more monCy than what I saved through my life. What could I do? Would all my efforts for sixteen long years go in vain? Many people came forward with their mite. My wife Bela wanted to sell everything she had to add to our sav- ings. My son wanted to get loan from his work-place. My friend (X) Dhuijatl Prasad Gupta came to donate Rs. 5000.00 to the ‘Ramayana Printing Fund’! Ms. Rajlaxml Chaudhuri offered her bangles. Putuldi, a retired teacher living on her meagre pension, came quietly with Rs. 301.00 to help me. My eyes get wet when I think of jQl the kind- ness of the people that rained upon me to cool my worries. I re- quested everyone to wait till I could gather courage enough to launch this publishing project which might turn out heavier than 1 could bear. Balaram Santra of Kalyan Ashram, Agartala was one of the few quiet admirers who would like to see the Ramayana in print. At his request Kripa Prasad Slnghji of All India Vanbasi Kalyan Ashram. Jashpur made endeavours for a whole year to find out some benevo-

lent sponsor to donate some mon^ to help publish the Ramayana for the benefit of the tribal people of Tripura. But God willed not that way. In this grave crisis also He gave me courage not to lose heart and to say, "Thy will be done.’ Meanwhile I got a commission to translate the third volume of Sri Rajmala into English. Sri Rajmala is the history of Tripura and her Kings written in Bangla rhyming couplets by Gangadhar Siddhanta Bagish in the 1 7“* century. I rendered it into English verse line by line. It was published in 1995. 1 wsis asked by an esoteric group to translate into Kakbarak the gem of a booklet, 'Manav Dharma’, an edited version of an enlightening lecture delivered by a young Re- search Scholar in Chicago. U.S.A. in 1933. The speaker has grown to be the scholar-extraordinary and saint, Mahanambrata Brahmachari. I did. It will be published soon. When the state of affairs was in such toteil confusion my friends asked me to approach the Ministers. But I could not do so. My rea- sons may sound foolish to many. But 1 have confessed already that I had been less intelligent than everyone: it ran in the family. 1 con- fess again that I have been a Lotus Eater all through my life. 1 lived in a sort of dreamland, far from reality. I did not pay heed to ray counselors who advised me not to waste my time and energy in this unreal, unworkable, good for-nothing venture. So 1 am now at this juncture. I have wasted my genius and my youth, 1 denied my family the happiness that money can buy and now 1 am nowhere. If the Ramayana cannot be published for want of money the termites would

feed upon the manuscript. No one will know about it. Yet it is a unique work. The Ramayana has been translated into many of the large world languages. But of the hundreds of tribal languages of the world not even one has a complete Ramayana in it. If published, my Kakbarak Ramayana in verse could make history. Another five hundred years would pass for another Lotus Eater to be born, to waste his youth and genius, to work with the Ramayana with his (xl) indefatigable optimism, to try to help Kakbarak to develop, and when his work will be complete, to And the government publishing organ suddenly turn cool and his manuscript become good for nothing. I should have tried to meet the Ministers; I could not. Agartala is a small place. Itiere are advantages and disadvantages of living in a small place. Advantages are that there almost everyone is known to others. The present Chief Minister was my student in his college days. The present Education Minister was a very good friend. 1 can go to meet them without much effort and request them to help me out of my crisis. It is possible that they would. But there is a disad- vantage also. There could be some difficulty for which they might not help me. I would irrationally think that they did not help me although they could. So the Lotus Eater in me did not permit me to approach the Ministers for help. Wordsworth would not go to visit Yarrow lest the picture he painted in his heart of Yarrow be broken at the touch of reality. 1 did not go fo approach the highest authori- ties in the government for the same reeison. I would rather keep the

belief in my heart that they would help me if 1 did ask for it. By July 1998 my stars seemed to change their position in the con- stellation. My crisis began to recede. As I am due to retire in Febru- ary 2000, I got my gratuity, provident fund, savings etc. calculated to see whether the whole amount would be adequate for the printing of the Ramayana. Then I and my wife went to Subal Kumar De, the Editor of the Syandan Patrlka. He has always been a younger brother to me. We told him everything and wanted to know the position; the money that 1 expected t© get vis-a-vis the expenditure to be incurred in the printing. My wife added that he was not merely a brother-in- law, he was like a son to her. The calculations should be very real. We have no other means to meet any unforeseen shortfall. He smiled and said something the like of which nobody else could say. He said, “Don’t worry. It will be printed. It is a national duty. Everyone should help. Give it to me It will be done.” The burden of the Himalayas, as it were, was taken off from my chest. Tlie work began. About a week after that Agni Kumar Acharjee, the retired Deputy Secretary of Tripura Public Service Commlslon and Gaurdas Saha of Parul Prakashani came to me on a certain errand. The Ramayana cropped up during conversation. 1 told them everything including our meeting Subal Kumar De. They were interested. They told me that they would try to help me. Gaurdas said that it would be diffi- cult to publish a 600 page book from Agartala. Agni Babu and Gaurdas apprised Mr. Jauhourie, the Station Director, Door Darshan Kendra. Agartala of my Ramayana. He was very kind to take Interest

in the matter. He got an interview with me about my Ramayana. It (xli) was later telecast from Agartala Kendra. 1 told Subal about Gaurdas’ apprehension. He appreciated and stopped the work at Agartala. The scene shifted to Calcutta. All this happened in quick succession - as if in a dream. Gaurdas took the charge of the whole thing auid got it done. He led me through the darkness to light. When 1 was very young cmd my father was only a casual visitor to our house 1 was under the charge of my grandmother. She was my mentor and she moulded my character as she wanted. 1 do not re- member her figure very well today. But I have many of her sayings imprinted in my soul. 1 follow her instructions instinctively. She asked me to bow my head to all places of worship irrespective of the religion. She advised me never to ask for anything from God be- cause He is so big a giver that whaterver I ask for would appear ridiculously trivial. She instructed me to pray to God to keep every- one happy so that no one would need to seek my help which 1 may not be able to render. She asked me to be always content because God is always just and He gives everyone according to his needs and as he deserves. I am content. 1 have come through many vicissitudes. Yet 1 am con- tent. What is life if there is no battle to fight? 1 fought, lost and won. I have a darling of a daughter, a sagacious son, both happily mar- ried. The son-in-law, Basab and the daughter-in-law, Mudita are delectable persons 1 have a jewel of a grandson, my daughter’s son,

Sanket. 1 have my two devoted brothers - Dipankar and Krittlbas - and their families. 1 have am uncompromising, undemanding wife to look after me through weal and woe. 1 have numberless friends and well wishers. 1 have no enemies. Enemies are bom of wealth and power and I have none. 1 bear no ill will to anybody. 1 adways try to “take praise and reproach alike, remain in contemplation and be contented in anything and everything." tidyanindilsIxitiTrnaimi santusto yena kenachit My Ramayana is finally printed. Thanks to the composers amd the printers. They did a marvelous job in an unknown language. 1 hope all that 1 meamt it for will come tme. Kaikbarak speakers will read ir centuries after my generation will have sunk into oblivion. 1 shaU retire In Februairy 2000. Vanaprastha at laist. 1 do not know how mamy days are left in my life’s acount. Given the time 1 have the desire to constmct a Kakbauak - Bamgla amd a Bangla - Kadcbaraik Dlctlonauy. 1 also intend to work for a Comprehensive Graunmau- of the Chaikma Lamguaige. 1 only wish. I shadl have time for aill that. Should summons come before 1 complete the works 1 shadl leave them for someone else to do. (xill) I say to everyone : Thank you I am grateful to you for all the kind words and deeds you said and did unto me. 1 say to the maker of eveiyone : Thy will be done - Kanshye vachanang taba. JAIRAM Mahashivaratri
